patient.chief_complaint: Acute quadriplegia, decreased consciousness, and aphasia discovered postoperatively in the recovery unit
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Priya Krishnamurthy is a 34-year-old right-handed woman who was transferred to the intensive care unit approximately 6 hours following an otherwise uneventful exploratory laparotomy performed under general anesthesia for evaluation of recurrent right upper quadrant abdominal pain suspected to be related to chronic cholecystitis. The surgical procedure lasted approximately 90 minutes and was reported as uncomplicated, with stable hemodynamics throughout and no episodes of hypotension or hypoxia noted on the anesthesia record. In the post-anesthesia care unit, the nursing staff noted that the patient was not recovering consciousness as expected. She was noted to have no purposeful movement of any extremity, was making only incomprehensible sounds, and was not following commands. The surgical team initially attributed the findings to prolonged effects of general anesthesia, but after 3 hours without improvement, a neurology consultation was requested. On evaluation by the neurology team, the patient was found to have a Glasgow Coma Scale of 8, profound quadriparesis with only trace movement in the upper extremities and no movement in the lower extremities, absent deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. She appeared globally aphasic. A review of her preoperative assessment confirmed that she was neurologically intact, conversant, and ambulatory independently prior to surgery. Her medical history is notable for type 2 diabetes managed with metformin and glibenclamide, and hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. A review of her medical records reveals a prior episode of bilateral lower extremity numbness approximately 2 years ago that lasted 5 days and was attributed to lumbar radiculopathy, and an episode of transient blurry vision in the right eye 8 months ago attributed to dry eye. Both episodes resolved spontaneously. The acute and severe nature of the presentation in the post-surgical setting raises immediate concern for a perioperative vascular event such as spinal cord infarction, cerebrovascular accident, or a structural lesion unmasked by the physiological stress of surgery.

results.title: Tumefactive demyelinating lesions: clinical features and outcomes with high-dose corticosteroids
results.summary: Retrospective study of 168 patients with biopsy-proven tumefactive demyelination. 70% showed significant clinical and radiographic improvement within 2-4 weeks of IV methylprednisolone pulse therapy (1g/day for 5 days). Early and dramatic response to steroids is a hallmark feature distinguishing tumefactive MS from CNS neoplasms.

results.title: Tumefactive demyelinating disease: clinical, imaging, treatment, and outcome features
results.summary: Review of tumefactive MS highlighting that open ring enhancement on MRI, response to corticosteroid pulse therapy, and young age of onset are key diagnostic features. Approximately 60-70% of tumefactive MS cases can be diagnosed without brain biopsy when clinical and radiological features are characteristic.

results.title: Distinguishing tumefactive demyelination from brain tumors: role of MR spectroscopy and corticosteroid response
results.summary: MR spectroscopy combined with clinical response to high-dose corticosteroids can differentiate tumefactive demyelination from neoplasm in most cases. Demyelinating lesions show moderate choline elevation (unlike marked elevation in glioma), elevated myoinositol, and reduced NAA, and typically show dramatic improvement after steroid therapy.

output.summary: IV corticosteroid pulse therapy has been used in suspected tumefactive demyelination; a dramatic clinical and radiographic response to steroids is considered a hallmark feature that distinguishes tumefactive MS from CNS neoplasms. MR spectroscopy can provide supporting evidence. If no response to steroids is seen within 2-4 weeks, brain biopsy should be considered.

results.title: Tumefactive demyelination presenting as acute neurological deterioration after surgery
results.summary: Case series of 5 patients with previously undiagnosed demyelinating disease who presented with acute neurological deterioration in the perioperative period. General anesthesia and surgical stress may unmask or exacerbate subclinical CNS demyelinating disease. The physiological stress of surgery may trigger an acute MS relapse.

results.title: Tumefactive demyelinating lesions mimicking brain tumor: diagnostic and therapeutic approach
results.summary: Review of 26 cases of tumefactive MS initially misdiagnosed as brain tumors. Key distinguishing features include: open ring enhancement (vs. closed ring in GBM), younger patient age, multifocal lesions, negative CSF cytology, and dramatic corticosteroid response. Up to 40% of tumefactive MS cases initially undergo unnecessary brain biopsy.

output.summary: Tumefactive MS can present acutely in the perioperative period and frequently mimics brain tumors on initial imaging. Surgical stress and general anesthesia are recognized triggers for acute MS relapses. Key diagnostic features that distinguish tumefactive MS from neoplasm include open ring enhancement, MR spectroscopy pattern, negative CSF cytology, and dramatic response to corticosteroid pulse therapy.

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no role in MS diagnosis — findings are non-specific and do not contribute to dissemination in space or time.
CT is markedly inferior to MRI for visualising demyelinating plaques; ordering CT delays diagnosis and adds radiation without clinical benefit.
No cardiac indication in a typical MS workup; echocardiography does not inform the demyelinating differential.
Cardiac monitoring is only indicated for first-dose fingolimod initiation (bradyarrhythmia risk) — not as part of MS diagnostic workup.

sequence_constraints.reason: Standard pre-LP imaging: confirm absence of mass effect / herniation risk on brain MRI before lumbar puncture

critical_actions: Establish dissemination in space (DIS) using brain and spinal-cord MRI in MS-typical regions (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord)
Establish dissemination in time (DIT) by demonstrating simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, a new lesion on follow-up MRI, or CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (per McDonald 2017)
Exclude NMOSD and MOGAD with AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG cell-based assays before committing to an MS diagnosis and DMT
Order CSF analysis with paired serum to assess oligoclonal bands and IgG index
For tumefactive presentations with mass effect, consult neurosurgery and consider brain biopsy if imaging plus CSF/serology do not establish diagnosis with confidence
Treat the acute relapse with high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3–5 days), with plasma exchange reserved for steroid-refractory severe relapses
Initiate a disease-modifying therapy (DMT) after relapse stabilization; choice between platform vs. high-efficacy agent based on disease activity, MRI burden, and patient preference
Check JC virus antibody serostatus before considering natalizumab; verify up-to-date vaccinations (especially live-attenuated) before initiating B-cell depleting or S1P-modulator DMTs
Counsel on Uhthoff phenomenon, heat avoidance, smoking cessation, and vitamin D supplementation as modifiable lifestyle factors
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting McDonald 2017 criteria and excluding mimics
Do not start natalizumab in a JC virus-antibody-positive patient (especially with high index) without explicit benefit-risk discussion of PML
Do not initiate fingolimod without a baseline ECG and first-dose bradyarrhythmia monitoring; avoid in patients with second-degree AV block, prior MI, or severe sleep apnea
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as a maintenance treatment for MS — they are ineffective long-term and carry significant harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal-cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS criteria — cord lesions change relapse counting and management

Do not pursue aggressive cytoreductive surgery for a presumed tumefactive demyelinating lesion before exhausting non-invasive workup — open ring enhancement, CSF OCBs, and AQP4/MOG serology should be obtained first
key_reasoning_points: MS is a clinical-radiographic diagnosis: McDonald 2017 requires dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT) plus exclusion of better explanations — no single test confirms it

MS-typical MRI regions are periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord — recognising a lesion in three of these regions establishes DIS for an attack-meeting clinical event
CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (≥2 bands not present in paired serum) can substitute for DIT under McDonald 2017 when DIS is met — this changes the calculus for clinically isolated syndromes

Short-segment (<2 vertebral bodies), peripheral, dorsolateral or dorsal-column spinal cord lesions strongly favour MS over NMOSD (which characteristically produces longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis ≥3 segments)

Tumefactive demyelinating lesions are a recognised MS variant — distinguishing imaging features from neoplasm include open ring enhancement, prominent intralesional venules, less mass effect than expected for size, and CSF OCBs; brain biopsy should be a last resort
Open-ring enhancement with the opening oriented toward the cortex is a high-specificity sign of demyelination, distinguishing tumefactive MS from neoplasm and abscess
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG must be ordered as cell-based assays, not ELISA — the older ELISA-based AQP4 assays have unacceptable false-negative rates
T1 hypointense 'black holes' indicate axonal loss from prior inflammatory episodes and contribute evidence of dissemination in time even without simultaneous enhancing lesions

Choice of DMT — platform agent (interferon-β, glatiramer, teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate) vs. high-efficacy agent (natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, cladribine, S1P modulators) — should weigh disease activity, MRI burden, patient comorbidities, JCV serostatus, and reproductive plans
If the initial brain MRI does not include the spinal cord, extending imaging to cervical and thoracic cord is essential — both for diagnostic DIS and for relapse counting

Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: McDonald 2024: dissemination in space and time is established on MRI, and oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time rather than being required — the reviewers' point.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: acute postoperative presentation mimics stroke or brain tumor. The large ring-enhancing posterior fossa lesion strongly suggests glioblastoma. CSF is entirely normal (no oligoclonal bands), removing a typical MS diagnostic clue. Prior demyelinating episodes were misattributed to other conditions. Diagnosis requires recognizing the open ring enhancement pattern, obtaining MR spectroscopy, and observing dramatic steroid response.
